title: Vishnu at Bali's door
hookLine: a king who lost everything gets a guard at his door, and a visit home that Kerala gets ready for
carry: grace took the throne, then guarded the door
tomorrow: a baby cries by a river, a bell at his neck. whose son is he?

cards: Where do you send a king who has just lost the three worlds? Bali was left bound, his head under the foot of the giant Vamana. A story could end there, with the proud one humbled.
The Bhagavata Purana doesn't. And Kerala doesn't either. On an Onam morning in Kerala, someone is on their knees at the front door, laying flower petals into a circle, ring by ring.
In the way Kerala tells it, they're getting ready for a guest.

teach.h: I TAKE THE WEALTH OF THOSE I FAVOR
teach.b: In the Bhagavata, Bali's grandfather Prahlada arrives, and Bali's wife pleads for him. And Vishnu explains himself.

When I favor someone, he says, I take away their wealth, because pride in wealth makes a person stiff, deaf to the world and to me. Hindus call God's favor anugraha, grace, and here it looks exactly like loss.
Then Vishnu gives Bali a new home, a realm under the earth called Sutala, a place of comfort and peace.
And he makes a startling promise: he will stand at Bali's door himself, mace in hand, guarding him. The god who took the worlds becomes the doorkeeper of the king who gave them.
Teachers love this picture: God, who needs nothing, bound by love to a devotee. Here Kerala adds what the Bhagavata doesn't say.
Tradition in Kerala says Bali asked for one more thing: to come back and see his people once a year. Onam is that visit.

So people get ready the way you'd get ready for someone you love, and the way the Upanishads say to treat any guest: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. The flower carpet at the door is the pookalam.

The great meal, the sadya, is served on a banana leaf, dish after dish in its place, and families sit down together to eat it. New clothes, games, boat races, songs. Losing the throne wasn't the end of Bali.
In this telling, it was grace.

how: At Onam, families in Kerala lay a pookalam of flower petals at the door, wear new clothes and share the sadya, a feast served on a banana leaf, to welcome Mahabali on his visit to his people.

games.q: what does “kerala's onam and ayyappa” mean?
o: a festival marking the day Bali was sent below the earth
a festival welcoming Bali home on his visit each year
a festival where Vishnu's mace is carried door to door

games.q: after the third step — tap the pairs.
p: Bali's new home below the earth
a flower carpet at the door
a feast served on a banana leaf

s: the Bhagavata Purana ends Bali's story with him humiliated
Vishnu gives him Sutala and promises to guard his door himself.
the yearly visit home comes from Kerala's tradition, not the Bhagavata
the Bhagavata doesn't mention it; Kerala tradition says Bali asked to see his people once a year.
in the Bhagavata, Vishnu says taking a person's wealth can be his favor
pride in wealth makes a person stiff, so taking it away can be grace, anugraha.

games.q: you're Vishnu. you've taken the three worlds from Bali in two steps, and he's offered his head for the third. what do you give him?
o: a new home, and you yourself as his guard.
games.why: in the Bhagavata, Vishnu says taking wealth can be a favor that frees from pride, then gives Bali the realm of Sutala and promises to stand at his door, mace in hand.

practice: With each slow breath, lay down one ring of petals, the way a pookalam is built from the center out: one ring for the people in your home, one for your street, one for someone you haven't seen in a long time.
Keep going until the circle feels wide enough, then rest in the middle of it. If you pray, offer the circle to Vishnu, who keeps Bali's door.

wordCard.voice: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, Bali's reward: Vishnu guards his door, and Kerala welcomes him home each Onam with flowers and a feast. Today's word.

orig.note: Malayalam, the language of Kerala: Onam, the festival that welcomes Mahabali home.

carryVoice: Your line: grace took the throne, then guarded the door. The god who took the worlds stands guard for the giver. Flowers at the door, and that's today.
